EDS AI Workflow (Forge)

Developer harness (Forge)

Forge is the EDS developer harness for building features with AI coding agents. It takes a user story from the handed-off product requirements document (PRD) through six stages: Clarify, Specify, Slice, Implement, Verify and Retrospect. A person signs off the specification and the tickets before any code is written.

Forge builds on Matt Pocock’s engineering skills for planning and implementation, and adds its own skills for coding, review and verification. The six stages are a recommended starting point, not a fixed process; teams can adapt them to their project.

AIHow AI can help in this chapter

  • Sharpen the plan

  • Collect review evidence

Set up the harness once

Each repository is set up once, before delivery work starts. The developer installs Matt Pocock’s engineering skills and the Forge skills, including the IM8 review skill, which ships separately.

  • Configure the repository. Matt Pocock’s /setup-matt-pocock-skills records where issues live, the triage labels and where domain documents go. The Clarify, Specify and Implement skills depend on this configuration.
  • Optionally, seed the coding standards file. A CODING_STANDARDS.md file that points to the /code-minimum rules lets the code review check those rules from the first feature. Later, /retro adds rules to the file.
  • Keep shared standards to hand. The AppStandards library of application best-practice documents, on topics such as logging and access control, remains available as guidance. It is not part of the definition of done.

The developer runs Forge locally and works with the agent interactively, reviewing and directing its work as it goes.

See the six stages

Clarify and Specify turn one user story into a specification, and a person signs it off. Slice breaks the specification into small tickets, and a person signs those off too. Implement builds every ticket, Verify reviews the result and tests the user stories end to end, and Retrospect feeds lessons into the next cycle.

The six stages, their skills and results
StageSkillsResult
1. Clarify/wayfinder or /grill-with-docsResolved decisions, recorded as architecture decision records (ADRs) and a glossary
2. Specify/to-specA specification on the issue tracker, signed off by a person
3. Slice/to-ticketsSmall tickets with their dependencies, signed off by a person
4. Implement/implement-spec, following /code-minimumEvery ticket built and tested on one integration branch
5. Verify/thermo-nuclear-review and /im8-review, then /e2eReview findings fixed and end-to-end evidence for each user story
6. Retrospect/retroProposed improvements to rules, checks and skills

1. Clarify the story

Clarify resolves the story’s open questions before anything is written down. The developer chooses one of two Matt Pocock skills, depending on how well the story is understood.

Clarify skills
SkillUse it whenWhat it does
/wayfinderThe story is large or unclear, too big for one agent sessionCharts the work on the issue tracker as decision tickets and resolves them one at a time until the route is clear.
/grill-with-docsThe story is well definedInterviews the developer to stress-test the plan, and records ADRs and a glossary as it goes.

Settle two things here: what not to build, and which new libraries to add. Record library choices as ADRs. Tickets are built in parallel later, so two tickets could otherwise add two libraries that do the same job.

AIHow AI can help

Give the agent the user story, the PRD and the repository. It can question the plan and draft decision records. The developer checks each decision against the story and the domain, and keeps the agreed ADRs and glossary in the repository.

2. Specify the change

/to-spec turns the decisions from Clarify into a specification, the user-story technical requirements document (TRD), and publishes it to the issue tracker.

Sign-off 1 A person reviews the specification and signs it off before slicing starts. Requested changes go back into the specification.

3. Slice the work into tickets

/to-tickets breaks the approved specification into tracer-bullet tickets: thin vertical slices, each delivering a working piece of the story through every layer it needs. Each ticket lists the tickets that block it, so the set forms a task graph for Implement.

Sign-off 2 A person reviews the tickets and signs them off before implementation starts. Requested changes go back into the slicing.

AIHow AI can help

The agent can draft the specification and slice it into tickets with their dependencies. The reviewer checks that the tickets cover the approved specification, that each is small and demonstrable, and that the dependencies are right, then records the sign-off.

4. Implement the tickets

/implement-spec builds the whole specification on one integration branch. Each ticket gets a fresh implementer agent that builds it test-first. The run ends with a code review against the repository’s coding standards and the specification, and a final pass fixes what the review finds.

While they write code, implementers follow the Forge /code-minimum rules. These favour the least new code: avoid unneeded work, then reuse what the codebase already has, then framework features, then installed libraries, and write custom code only as a last resort.

/implement-spec runs once for the specification; it is not a repeating loop. It replaces the earlier Forge /do-work loop, which has been retired.

AIHow AI can help

Build the approved tickets and report what passed

Implement connects each ticket to its tests and the closing code review, so the developer can inspect evidence rather than rely on a completion claim.

Give AI
The approved specification and tickets, the ADRs from Clarify and the repository’s coding standards.
AI helps by
Building each ticket test-first, reusing existing code where it can, and fixing the code review’s findings.
People check
The developer inspects the code and tests against the tickets and reruns the important checks.
Keep as evidence
The integration branch, test results and the code review’s findings and fixes.

5. Verify the result

Verify runs independent reviews on the integration branch, then tests the user stories end to end. Fix what the reviews find before moving on.

Verify skills
SkillMaintained byWhat it checks
/thermo-nuclear-reviewCursorMaintainability, very strictly: abstraction quality, oversized files and tangled conditions, with restructurings that make the code simpler.
/im8-reviewCoreX EDS teamThe 36 IM8 application technical controls. It rates each control pass, fail, warning or not applicable, lists items for manual review and writes a compliance report.
/e2eCoreX EDS teamTurns each user story into repeatable Playwright browser tests, with video and trace evidence. A stability run repeats the tests to catch results that change between runs.

The developer starts the maintainability review by hand; the agent does not run it on its own. /e2e reads user stories and their acceptance criteria from files in the repository, so commit the stories you want tested.

AIHow AI can help

The review skills can flag maintainability and security issues, and /e2e can turn stories into browser tests. Reviewers check each finding against the cited code and rerun the tests. Keep the reports and test evidence with the story.

6. Retrospect and improve the setup

/retro reviews the session after each feature, or whenever a run went badly, and suggests changes to the agent’s environment. Lessons from one story then improve the next.

  • Mechanical mistakes: a new linter rule or hook, so the same mistake fails a check next time.
  • Judgement calls: a new entry in the coding standards file, which the code review checks from then on.
  • Gaps in guidance: better documentation or skills.

To trace a failure to its cause, use the harness diagnosis method in the overview.

Definition of done

A story is done when the following hold. Teams that adapt the stages should adapt this list to match.

  • Open decisions are resolved and recorded as ADRs.
  • Sign-off 1 The specification is reviewed and signed off before slicing.
  • Sign-off 2 The tickets are reviewed and signed off before implementation.
  • Every ticket is built test-first, and the code review’s findings are fixed.
  • The maintainability and IM8 reviews have run on the integration branch, and their findings are fixed.
  • End-to-end tests pass for the story, with fresh evidence.

Then run /retro and act on what it finds before the next story.
